description.narrative:
1. To ensure that the Netherlands respects its international commitments in foreign aid and makes sure more resources go to the people who need them most. More concretely, the outcomes of this project are:
1.1 Defending the ODA contribution to development relevant fields and increased allocation for LDCs To achieve these primary results, the consortium will contribute to a strong civil society and active citizenship, especially from youth in the Netherlands, that, in turn, contributes to the desired systemic change by raising awareness and advocating for ODA to be spent on tackling the global challenges on different topics with the Sustainable Development Goals as guideline. These challenges—for instance, Loss and Damage issues within the greater Climate context—disproportionately affect Low and Middle Income Countries (LMICs). A higher proportion of resources, therefore, must be allocated to address the consequences of these global challenges in LMICs instead of going toward in-donor refugee costs in the Netherlands.
1.2 Increased public support for ODA in the Netherlands, with a focus on young people Public support greatly influences political representatives and the political agenda. The project aims to get people interested in a technical issue, such as ODA, and to understand how minimal effort from the government (meeting the commitment of spending 0,7% GDP on ODA) could lead to maximum impact on global issues like climate change or global health, even at home in the Netherlands. The project will leverage the engagement of political engaged youth through the political youth chapters and existing youth movements that advocate for climate and social justice to build a shared understanding of development aid allocation policies and to act as part of a global network of youth movements.

Recently a new government was installed with four political parties (PVV, VVD, NSC, BBB) in the Netherlands. The new minister for Foreign Trade and Aid, Reinette Klever, is from the extreme right-wing party PVV and the new minister of Foreign Affairs, Caspar Veldkamp, is from the new political party NSC. In the main line agreement severe cuts have been announced on ODA starting with 300 million in 2025, 500 million in 2026, to a structural 2,4 billion in 2027/2028. On top of these severe cuts, additional cuts to the budget of Foreign Trade and Aid are expected for 2025 and 2026 due to higher in-donor refugee costs. From 2027 a cap of 10% on in-donor refugee costs will be introduced. For 2027/2028 most of the structural cut of 2,4 billion will be in-donor refugee costs considering the forecasts on in-donor refugee costs. After these cuts take effect, in-donor refugee costs will be paid out of the general budget. This means that the ODA percentage will decline rapidly but the ODA budget will be more development relevant since absolutely and relatively less will be spent on in-donor refugee costs. Apart from the huge impact on the Dutch development budget, we also expect other problematic policies by the new government, for example on migration, international climate policies and the Dutch global health policy. But since many of the new plans still need to be worked out, the exact consequences will become clear later this year, or only in 2025. For example, a new policy framework for development aid will be launched in the first quarter of 2025.
